q: Rank Madeira's four classic noble varieties from driest to sweetest, and name the grape behind most of the island's wine.
accept: sercial verdelho bual malmsey and tinta negra
sercial verdelho boal malvasia with tinta negra
sercial verdelho bual malvasia tinta negra is the workhorse
driest sercial then verdelho bual malmsey plus tinta negra
ans: Sercial (driest), Verdelho, Boal/Bual, then Malvasia/Malmsey (sweetest); Tinta Negra supplies roughly 80-85% of the crop
exp: The ladder describes where fermentation is arrested, not an inherent sweetness in the grape, though the varieties are planted to suit it — Sercial highest and coolest on the north side, Malvasia lowest and warmest in the south. Terrantez and Bastardo are the rare, treasured extras. A named variety must be at least 85% of the wine; since 2015 the black-skinned Tinta Negra may finally be named on the label rather than hiding behind the old sweetness terms (Dry, Medium Dry, Medium Rich, Rich), which is how most Madeira still reaches the shelf.

q: Within what window after the harvest must Late Bottled Vintage Port be bottled, and what separates the two styles on the shelf?
accept: four to six years then either filtered or unfiltered bottle matured
bottled in the fourth to sixth year filtered or bottle matured
4 to 6 years in wood filtered ready to drink or unfiltered needing a decant
bottled between the fourth and sixth year after harvest with filtered lbv ready to pour and bottle matured unfiltered
ans: Bottled between the fourth and sixth year after harvest (1 July of year four to 31 December of year six). Most is filtered and ready to pour; unfiltered 'Bottle Matured' LBV gets at least three further years in bottle before release and throws a sediment
exp: LBV was devised to give something of Vintage character without the twenty-year wait, and the two versions are almost different drinks. The filtered, cold-stabilised majority is a by-the-glass workhorse that will not improve much; the unfiltered kind (Warre's Traditional, Smith Woodhouse, Niepoort) behaves like a junior Vintage, needs decanting, and rewards a decade. Contrast the wood regimes an examiner will chain onto this: Vintage takes about two years in cask then all its life in glass, Colheita seven-plus years in wood, Crusted a multi-year blend bottled unfiltered.

q: The Douro sub-region with the largest vineyard area, and the source of most Vintage Port, is:
exp: Cima Corgo, centred on Pinhao and the Torto and Pinhao tributaries, holds the highest concentration of A-graded parcels and most of the classified quintas — Bomfim at Pinhao, Malvedos at Tua and Noval above Pinhao all sit within it, while Taylor's Vargellas lies further east, beyond the Cachao da Valeira, in the Douro Superior. Baixo Corgo is the westernmost and wettest, the most densely planted but supplying lighter wine for young ruby and tawny; Douro Superior runs east to the Spanish border, hottest and driest, least planted and the modern expansion frontier (Vesuvio, Vale Meao). Tras-os-Montes is the neighbouring DOC to the north and makes no Port at all.

q: How does a vin de liqueur differ from a vin doux naturel in construction, and name two vins de liqueur.
accept: vdl is spirit into unfermented must pineau des charentes and floc de gascogne
a mistelle of must and spirit such as pineau and macvin
vin de liqueur fortifies unfermented must while vdn stops a ferment
pineau des charentes floc de gascogne macvin made from unfermented must
spirit goes into unfermented must whereas a vdn has a running ferment arrested
ans: A vin doux naturel is fermented part-way and then arrested with neutral spirit; a vin de liqueur is a mistelle — spirit added to unfermented or barely fermented must, so it keeps its grape sugar and barely ferments at all. Pineau des Charentes, Floc de Gascogne, Macvin du Jura, Ratafia Champenois
exp: The spirit is regionally matched by law, which is the elegant part: Cognac goes into Pineau, Armagnac into Floc, marc du Jura into Macvin. A vin doux naturel is held to 15-18% alcohol, while a vin de liqueur usually lands higher, around 16-22%. The blind tell is aromatic — a vin de liqueur smells of grape juice and the spirit that stopped it, never of fermentation, where a VDN carries the winey, oxidative rancio of Maury, Banyuls or Rivesaltes. Note the mutage contrast the bank already teaches: 96% neutral spirit for VDN against Port's 77% aguardente.
